"Bidding" has two completely separate meanings as a noun. They come from two different uses of the verb "bid," and the meanings are so different that you must always figure out from context which one is being used.

In this sense, "bidding" means the orders, instructions, or wishes of someone who expects to be obeyed. It describes what a person in power — or a person who acts as if they are in power — wants done, and the expectation that someone else will carry it out.

Think of it this way: if a king commands a servant to fetch water, the servant is doing the king's bidding. The bidding is the command itself — not the action of fetching water, but the king's will and authority behind it.

Examples:

  • "She always does her mother's bidding, even when she disagrees." → She always follows and obeys her mother's orders.
  • "The assistant carried out his employer's bidding without question." → He followed every instruction his employer gave, without arguing.
  • "No one should have to do another person's bidding forever." → No one should have to live as someone else's obedient servant indefinitely.

Key phrases you must know:

  • "Do someone's bidding" — This is by far the most common phrase. It means to obey someone, to carry out their wishes or orders. "He did her bidding without hesitation."
  • "At someone's bidding" — This means "because someone ordered or commanded it." "At the director's bidding, the staff stayed late." It simply signals that someone's authority or instruction caused the action to happen.
  • "No one's bidding" — This means not obeying or acting at the command of any person. "She acted at no one's bidding — she followed only her own conscience."

Tone and nuance of this meaning:
This word carries a slightly old-fashioned or formal tone. It also often implies a power imbalance — the person doing the bidding is usually subordinate, and sometimes even resentful or unwilling. When someone says "I won't do your bidding," they are strongly asserting their independence and refusing to be controlled. The phrase feels heavier and more loaded than simply saying "I won't follow your instructions."
Meaning 2 — The act of making competitive offers (at an auction or similar context)

In this sense, "bidding" refers to the process in which people compete by offering prices to buy or win something. Each individual offer is called a bid, and the overall activity of multiple people making those offers is called the bidding.

You see this most commonly at auctions — where an item is sold to whoever offers the highest price. The bidding is the entire back-and-forth process of people calling out or submitting their prices.

Examples:

  • "The bidding started at $100 and quickly climbed to $4,000." → People began by offering $100, and the offers kept rising as more people competed.
  • "There was intense bidding for the rare diamond at the auction." → Many buyers competed fiercely, offering higher and higher prices.
  • "The bidding came to a close when no one topped the $25,000 offer." → No buyer was willing to go above $25,000, so that was the final winning offer.
  • "She won the painting after outlasting everyone else in the bidding." → She kept offering higher prices until all other competitors gave up.

Key phrases:

  • "The bidding opened / started at..." — The lowest initial offer at the beginning of an auction. "The bidding opened at $500."
  • "The bidding rose / climbed to..." — The offers kept increasing. "The bidding climbed to $20,000 in minutes."
  • "A bidding war" — A situation where two or more people or companies keep raising their offers, trying to outdo each other, often driving the price very high. "Two tech companies entered a bidding war for the startup." (You'll hear this in business news often.)
  • "Competitive bidding" — A formal process where multiple parties submit their best offer for a contract or project, and the best offer wins. Used heavily in business and government.

Where this meaning appears:

  • At live or online auctions (art, antiques, property, etc.)
  • On platforms like eBay, where buyers submit offers
  • In business, when companies compete to win a contract by submitting price proposals
  • In card games like Bridge, where "the bidding" refers to the opening phase of the game where players declare how many tricks they plan to win — though this specific use is narrow and you'll mainly see it if you play or read about that game
How to tell the two meanings apart

The context will almost always make it obvious.

If the sentence is about obeying a person — someone doing what another person told them to do — it's Meaning 1.
→ "He obeyed his master's bidding."

If the sentence is about offering money or competing to buy/win something — it's Meaning 2.
→ "The bidding reached $1 million at the auction."

The most important thing to hold onto is this: "bidding" always involves responding to someone or something. In Meaning 1, a person responds to another person's authority by obeying. In Meaning 2, buyers respond to an opportunity by offering money. Both senses carry the idea of an active response to a call — which is exactly why one word covers both ideas.
